Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations

Memory.value: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

vignette: Tane had never expected a routine highway stop to unravel his sense of safety. It was a Tuesday in November, the Pacific air thick, when a patrol vehicle flared behind his sedan. What frightened him most was the sudden physical proximity of the officer stepping into his window, his boots hitting the asphalt just as the car door unclicked. The radio crackled, a sharp, ordinary sound that made Tane jump before he even realized he had moved. He had come to believe that the officer's delayed explanation was not simply paperwork catching up, but a sign that something bad was happening inside the patrol car. Strangers approaching him, even in the most ordinary situations, now carry a quiet threat, and when the officer's hand rested too close on his shoulder, Tane felt a familiar turn of nausea in his gut. He knows the story felt unreal at the time, so extreme and sudden that it is hard to believe it actually happened to him, yet the memory arrives with a terror identical to the moment itself. More real than normal, the memory sits just beneath his skin, vivid and immediate. Over the weeks that followed, Tane's world narrowed. He noticed that driving with others felt different; when passengers occupied his backseat, the closeness of their breathing and the ordinary hum of the engine made his stomach twist. He avoided full cars, not because he disliked company, but because the physical proximity and the unspoken threat of a stranger drawing near made him certain that another delay would spiral into trouble. When a flight attendant took too long to hand him a boarding pass, or a maintenance check stretched past its scheduled time, Tane assumed something bad was happening, his posture stiffening as if bracing for the next approaching figure. The startle response followed him into the flight deck; a routine radio check, a dropped clipboard, even the soft click of a cabin door, made him jump. He stopped explaining himself too quickly, letting the silence stretch, watching the door. His life as an airline pilot became a study in careful observation. During a layover in Phoenix, Tane stood by the jet bridge, watching the ground crew move toward him. He did not move to meet them. The physical proximity of the crew chief stepping into his personal space sent a familiar wave of nausea across his abdomen, and Tane found himself stepping back, creating just enough room to breathe. He had come to believe that if he stayed too close to the boarding gate or let a co-pilot loom too near during pre-flight checks, the old terror would return. The habit of avoiding close quarters and waiting out delays accumulated quietly. His flight roster changed; he began requesting solo command rotations and driving to the airport alone, leaving his car empty behind him. The occupational consequence was subtle but steady: his crew noted his delayed sign-offs and his tendency to pause before answering, which gradually shifted how his captain and ground staff interacted with him. Now, at thirty-nine, Tane sits in his therapist's office, the heavy door closing behind him. He still watches the entrance, still feels the faint nausea when someone shifts in their seat too close. What frightened him most was not the event itself, but how quickly his body had learned to expect it again. He is here because the waiting, the startles, and the quiet threat of approaching strangers have begun to shape his days, and he hopes to find a way through the delay without assuming the worst. He is most afraid of being caught in another close encounter where time stretches and the body betrays him, yet he also hopes that learning to recognize the ordinary will allow him to step back into the sky without bracing for the storm.
